'''David Burton Wake''' (June 8, 1936 – April 29, 2021) was an American herpetologist. He was professor of [[biology|integrative biology]] and Director and curator of [[herpetology]] of the [[Museum of Vertebrate Zoology]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]]. Wake is known for his work on the biology and evolution of [[salamander]]s as well as general issues of vertebrate evolutionary biology.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Griesemer|first1=James |title=Integration of approaches in David Wake's model-taxon research platform for evolutionary morphology|journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part C: Studies in History and Philosophy of Biological and Biomedical Sciences|date=2013|volume=44|issue=4|pages=525–536|doi=10.1016/j.shpsc.2013.03.021|pmid=23588059 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|first=James R.|last= Griesemer|chapter=What Salamander Biologists Have Taught Us About Evo-devo|editor=Love, Alan C. |title=Conceptual Change in Biology|year=2015|publisher=Springer Netherlands|series= Boston Studies in the Philosophy and History of Science|volume= 307|number= 307|pages=271–300|doi= 10.1007/978-94-017-9412-1_13|isbn=978-94-017-9411-4}}</ref> He has served as president of the [[Society for the Study of Evolution]], the [[American Society of Naturalists]], and [[American Society of Zoologists]].  He was a member of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]], the [[Linnean Society of London]], the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]], the [[American Philosophical Society]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=David+B.+Wake&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-12-10|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> and in 1998 was elected into the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]]. He was awarded the 2006 [[Leidy Award]] from the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia.<ref name="PANSP">{{cite journal|date=June 2007|title=The Four Awards Bestowed by The Academy of Natural Sciences and Their Recipients|journal=Proceedings of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia|publisher=The Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia |volume=156 |issue=1 |pages=403–404 |doi=10.1635/0097-3157(2007)156[403:TFABBT]2.0.CO;2 |s2cid=198160356 }}<!--|access-date=15 April 2015--></ref>

== Early life ==
Wake was born in [[Webster, South Dakota]], and grew up in nearby [[Pierpont, South Dakota|Pierpont]].<ref name=DBW-Copeia>{{cite journal |last1=Staub |first1=Nancy L. |last2=Mueller |first2=Rachel Lockridge |title=David Burton Wake |journal=[[Copeia]] |date=2017 |volume=105 |issue=2 |pages=415–426 |doi=10.1643/ot-17-636 |s2cid=90792676 |url=https://wakelab.berkeley.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/50/2021/04/David-Burton-Wake.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|editor1-last=Henderson|editor1-first=Andrea Kovacs|title=American Men & Women of Science: A Biographical Directory of Today's Leaders in Physical, Biological, and Related Sciences|url=https://archive.org/details/americanmenwomen03hend|url-access=registration|date=2009|publisher=Gale|location=Detroit, Michigan|isbn=978-1414457260|page=[https://archive.org/details/americanmenwomen03hend/page/445 445]|edition=26th}}</ref> His mother was a high school biology teacher. He cited as a strong influence his maternal grandfather, a [[Lutheran]] pastor and amateur naturalist who took David on botanical walks and introduced him to Latin terminology and evolutionary principles. When Wake was in high school his family moved to [[Washington (state)|Washington state]] where he completed high school and enrolled in [[Pacific Lutheran College]], declaring a history major and considering a career in law. He soon decided to become a biologist instead, graduating in 1958, and chose to pursue graduate school at the [[University of Southern California]] under [[Jay M. Savage]]. He chose salamanders as a model of how species diversify, earning an M.S. in 1960 and PhD in 1964: writing his doctoral dissertation on the biology of [[lungless salamander]]s (family Plethodontidae).<ref name="Wake2010">{{cite journal|last1=Wake|first1=David B.|title=BIO|journal=Evolution & Development|date=2010|volume=12|issue=3|pages=244–245|doi=10.1111/j.1525-142X.2010.00409.x|pmid=20565534|s2cid=221679002}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
Wake was hired by the [[University of Chicago]] in 1964, where he worked until 1969, when he was hired as faculty member of UC Berkeley and curator of the [[Museum of Vertebrate Zoology]]. He served as director of the MVZ from 1971 to 1998.<ref name="Wake2010"/>  During his time as a graduate student, Wake met his future wife, [[Marvalee Wake|Marvalee Hendricks]], who was a student in a course he taught. She also became a graduate student in the Savage lab, and they married in 1962.<ref name="Wake2010"/> Their son, Thomas, is a [[zooarchaeologist]].<ref name=DBW-Copeia/><ref name="Sanders-2021"/> Along with [[Elizabeth Jockusch]], he identified several new species of [[Slender salamander|Batrachoseps salamanders]] in 2001.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jockusch|first1=Elizabeth L.|author-link=species:Elizabeth L. Jockusch|last2=Wake|first2=David B.|date=2002|title=Falling apart and merging: diversification of slender salamanders (Plethodontidae: Batrachoseps) in the American West|journal=Biological Journal of the Linnean Society|language=en|volume=76|issue=3|pages=361–391|doi=10.1046/j.1095-8312.2002.00071.x|issn=1095-8312|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Personal life ==
Wake died on April 29, 2021, at his home in Oakland, California.<ref name="Sanders-2021">{{cite web |last1=Sanders |first1=Robert |title=David Wake, a prominent herpetologist who warned of amphibian declines, is dead at 84 |url=https://news.berkeley.edu/2021/05/04/david-wake-a-prominent-herpetologist-who-warned-of-amphibian-declines-is-dead-at-84/ |website=Berkeley News |date=4 May 2021}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
Wake is commemorated in the names of the salamander ''[[Cryptotriton wakei]]'' (Wake's moss salamander), the skink genus ''[[Davewakeum]]'', the frog genus [[Wakea (genus)|''Wakea'']], a species of the [[Jurassic]] salamander ''[[Marmorerpeton]]'' and the lizard ''[[Cyrtodactylus wakeorum]]'' (Wakes' gecko)—the latter two named jointly after him and his wife.<ref name="BeolensWatkins2013">{{cite book|author=Beolens, Bo|author-link=species:Bo Beolens|author2=Watkins, Michael|author2-link=species:Michael Watkins|author3=Grayson, Michael|title=The Eponym Dictionary of Amphibians|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZZY3BAAAQBAJ&pg=PT355|year=2013|publisher=Exeter, England: Pelagic Publishing|isbn=978-1-907807-42-8|page=355}}</ref><ref name="BeolensWatkins2011">{{cite book|author1=Beolens, Bo|author2=Watkins, Michael|author3=Grayson, Michael|title=The Eponym Dictionary of Reptiles|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3ovZoFyLhzkC&pg=PT278|year=2011|publisher=Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press|isbn=978-1-4214-0135-5|pages=66, 278–279}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Bauer|first=Aaron M.|author-link=:fr:Aaron Matthew Bauer|year=2003|title= Descriptions of seven new ''Cyrtodactylus'' (Squamata: Gekkonidae) with a key to the species of Myanmar (Burma)|journal=Proceedings of the California Academy of Sciences|volume= 54|number=25|pages= 463–498|url=http://researcharchive.calacademy.org/research/Herpetology/myanmar/PDFS/proccas_v54_n25.pdf|quote=for their contributions to herpetology, vertebrate morphology, and evolutionary biology and for their valuable mentoring of many graduate students}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jones |first=Marc E. H. |last2=Benson |first2=Roger B. J. |last3=Skutschas |first3=Pavel |last4=Hill |first4=Lucy |last5=Panciroli |first5=Elsa |last6=Schmitt |first6=Armin D. |last7=Walsh |first7=Stig A. |last8=Evans |first8=Susan E. |date=2022-07-11 |title=Middle Jurassic fossils document an early stage in salamander evolution |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2114100119 |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=119 |issue=30 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2114100119 |issn=0027-8424|doi-access=free |pmc=9335269 }}</ref>

The specific epithet of the extinct ''[[Qikiqtania wakei]]'' was also given in his memory.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stewart |first=Thomas A. |last2=Lemberg |first2=Justin B. |last3=Daly |first3=Ailis |last4=Daeschler |first4=Edward B. |last5=Shubin |first5=Neil H. |date=August 2022 |title=A new elpistostegalian from the Late Devonian of the Canadian Arctic |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-022-04990-w |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=608 |issue=7923 |pages=563–568 |doi=10.1038/s41586-022-04990-w |issn=1476-4687|pmc=9385497 }}</ref>

David Wake was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] (1996), the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (1997), and the [[National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences of the United States]] (1998). He was a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim]] Fellow (1981 – 82) and was recipient of the Distinguished Herpetologist Award from the Herpetologists’ League (1984), the Grinnell Medal from the [[Museum of Vertebrate Zoology|MVZ]] (1998), the [[Henry S. Fitch]] Award from the [[American Society of Ichthyologists and Herpetologists]] (1999), the Joseph Leidy Medal of the [[Academy of Natural Sciences of Drexel University|Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia]] (2006) and the Fellows Medal of the [[California Academy of Sciences]] (2012).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bauer|first=Aaron M.|date=2021-12-27|title=David B. Wake (1936 – 2021), Salamander Specialist and Evolutionary Biologist|url=http://rjh.folium.ru/index.php/rjh/article/view/1874|journal=Russian Journal of Herpetology|volume=28|issue=6|pages=380–382|doi=10.30906/1026-2296-2021-28-6-380-382|s2cid=245527059 |issn=1026-2296|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In 1967, he received the [[Quantrell Award]].<ref name="Prize">{{cite web|title=Llewellyn John and Harriet Manchester Quantrell Awards for Excellence in Undergraduate Teaching|url=https://www.uchicago.edu/who-we-are/global-impact/accolades/llewellyn-john-and-harriet-manchester-quantrell-awards-for-excellence-in-undergraduate-teaching|website=UChicago}}</ref>
